IV. PRESENTATIONS: 
A. College and Career Readiness: From Aspiration to Action. The Superintendent and the College 
and Career Readiness team presented an overview of the district’s efforts to strengthen college 
and career readiness for students in Grades 6–12 through the My Career and Academic Plan 
(MyCAP) initiative. The presentation, titled “Aspiration to Action,” highlighted how student 
aspiration survey data informs secondary school pathways, counseling supports, and career-
connected learning experiences. The Superintendent emphasized that college and career readiness 
are complementary pathways that require transferable skills and preparation for future success. 
 
The team explained that MyCAP is supported through the SchoolLinks online platform and 
provides students with opportunities to establish goals and plan for life after high school. Results 
from the Class of 2026 aspiration survey showed that approximately 1,254 students completed the 
survey. Of those respondents, 66.8% planned to attend college, 8.7% intended to pursue a trade, 
7.9% planned to enter the workforce, 3.1% intended to enlist in the military, and 10.9% remained 
undecided. Among college-bound students, 25.8% had not determined their application approach, 
while 30.5% of respondents indicated that they had not taken the SAT but intended or needed to 
do so. The team explained that these results help counselors identify students who require 
additional guidance and targeted support to move forward with their plans. 
 
The presentation outlined the district’s comprehensive approach to college and career readiness, 
which begins in elementary grades and continues through high school. MyCAP activities address 
personal and social development, career exploration, and academic and postsecondary planning. 
Students participate in career interest inventories, college planning events, college visits, financial 
literacy activities, resume and essay writing, scholarship searches, and individualized advising. 
Additional support is provided to students and families based on identified needs, including 
assistance with financial aid and exploring alternative postsecondary pathways. 
 
The team also described how these efforts align with the district’s key performance indicators, 
including reading, mathematics, and writing proficiency; participation in advanced coursework,

assessments. School-based postsecondary success leadership teams will help monitor student 
progress and coordinate support to ensure that aspirations translate into meaningful opportunities 
and action. 
 
To illustrate the impact of these efforts, the team shared the experience of a senior at Putnam 
Vocational Academy who has pursued opportunities aligned with her interests in business and 
accounting. In Grade 10, she placed fifth nationally in a SkillsUSA and Microsoft competition. 
She later attended an Association of International Certified Professional Accountants-related 
conference at Clark University and was selected for a competitive paid summer experience in 
Boston, where she engaged with professionals from regional, national, and international firms. 
With support from her teacher and counselors, the student is now pursuing a cooperative work 
experience in accounting and exploring colleges aligned with her goals. 
The Committee thanked the College and Career Readiness team and student representatives for 
the presentation.

VII. REPORT OF THE SUPERINTENDENT: 
A. Superintendent Dr. Dinnall provided updates on district operations, community partnerships, 
academic initiatives, and the continued recovery of district technology systems following the 
recent cyber incident. 
 
The Superintendent recognized the district’s interpretation and translation services team. The team 
will provide interpretation services during full School Committee meetings, public speak-outs, 
upcoming town hall meetings, and district family engagement events, helping ensure that 
multilingual families can fully understand and participate in district activities. 
 
The Superintendent reported on recent engagement with Western New England University’s new 
president, Joseph Hartman, and expressed optimism about strengthening existing partnerships and 
expanding opportunities to additional schools throughout the district. She also acknowledged the 
participation of Springfield students and staff in the Puerto Rican Parade, celebrating the 
community’s cultural heritage and student involvement. 
Regarding the start of the school year, the Superintendent described visits to 42 schools on 
September 14, with the remaining schools visited on September 15. These visits allowed district 
leadership to observe teaching and learning, gather feedback from school staff, and address 
immediate needs. She commended principals, teachers, central office personnel, and support staff 
for their collaboration and timely response to requests for supplies and resources. The 
Superintendent also recognized the ongoing work of district and city technology teams to restore 
systems and return operations to normal following the cyber incident. 
 
The Superintendent highlighted progress in Advanced Placement (AP) programming, noting 
continued efforts to increase student participation and the number of students earning scores of

three or higher. She indicated that more detailed data would be shared with the School Committee 
at a future meeting and recognized the contributions of AP teachers, counselors, and families. 
 
The Superintendent also acknowledged the City’s continued investment in school facility 
improvements, including HVAC modernization at Friedman, Glenwood, and Glickman schools. 
She expressed appreciation for collaboration with union leadership and emphasized the 
importance of maintaining strong working relationships focused on student success. 
 
In discussing the district’s four strategic priorities, the Superintendent highlighted early literacy 
initiatives and professional learning through the Urban Superintendents Network. The district is 
exploring research and strategies to strengthen literacy instruction beginning in preschool and 
continuing through the early elementary grades, with the goal of ensuring that students read at 
grade level by the end of second grade. She noted that preliminary data showed promising 
progress and indicated that additional information would be shared with the Committee. 
 
The Superintendent reported that district learning walks had resumed, allowing leadership to 
observe Tier 1 instruction in classrooms. She praised the quality and rigor of instruction observed 
in several schools and specifically recognized South End Middle School for academic gains that 
outpaced state progress. She credited school leadership, staff, and district support for their 
sustained work and collaboration. 
 
The Superintendent also noted ongoing efforts to strengthen the district’s relationship with 
Westfield State University and announced the return of Super Saturdays and Super Sundays, 
beginning at Indian Orchard Elementary School. These events will include library partnerships, 
early literacy activities, and resources to help families support children’s readiness for 
prekindergarten through everyday activities and interactions. 
VIII. UNFINISHED BUSINESS 
IX. NEW BUSINESS 
A. Mayor Sarno recognized University of Massachusetts football players William “Pop” Watson III 
and Joseph Griffin Jr., both graduates of Central High School, for their contributions to the team’s 
strong start to the season. The mayor noted that UMass had begun the season 3–0 and credited the 
two Springfield graduates with helping generate renewed excitement around the program. He also 
recognized their family connections to Springfield Public Schools, noting that “Pop” Watson’s 
father coaches Central High School football and Joseph Griffin Sr. serves on the district’s security 
team. 
 
The Mayor and School Committee members also highlighted Central High School’s football 
program and its upcoming game against St. Sebastian’s School. They emphasized the importance 
of student-athletes succeeding academically as well as athletically and recognized the 
opportunities sports can provide for students to pursue higher education. Central student-athlete 
Isaiah Rogers was noted as an example of a student advancing to the collegiate level, with plans to 
attend the University of Notre Dame.
